Rejected alternatives

Merge WAL segments

Instead of reusing Kafka's storage system we could just merge WAL segments based on some heuristic. The problem here is two-fold:

  • With this we would create a competing and incompatible long-term storage system to the classic logs.
  • Finding a good heuristic for merging WAL segments is non-trivial. These heuristics can be for example:
    • Minimum and Maximum first-generation WAL Segment lifetime (~15 mins)
    • Grouping partitions by expected expiration time bucket (~1 day)
    • Maximum WAL Segment dirty ratios (50%)
    • Minimum and Maximum WAL Segment lifetime (~30 days)
    • Target WAL Segment size (~100MB) 

Further Improvements

Better remote log metadata manager

With the current design only by plugging in RLM, a bottleneck is possible when remote logs roll over too fast. __remote_log_metadata has 50 partitions by default and every broker needs to fetch subscribe to all because partitions are scattered across all of them. This means that we need to improve the tiered storage remote log metadata management, to solve these problems:

  • limit inter-broker metadata traffic: on high frequency rollover, metadata is generated fast, which may generate inter-zone traffic, thus defeating some of the cost savings given by diskless topics.
  • better compaction: the current remote metadata log isn't compacted at all, so it can grow huge
  • improve snapshotting: tiered storage metadata has no compaction and brokers need to replay the whole log

Since the metadata manager in tiered storage is pluggable, it's possible to implement a new one without changing interfaces that is better optimized for small remote log segments.

Topic Switching

Migrating classic topics to diskless have been mentioned in previous KIPs as it is an important feature. Switching classic topics to diskless would mean that there will be an offset chosen by the leader as the swtich-over point. From this point on logs are in diskless format and before that they are in classic format but they become consolidated diskless topics, so eventually these logs move to tiered storage while keeping their log format.

Glossary

Terms from KIP-1150 and KIP-1163 keep their meaning. The following are specific to this KIP:

  • Born-diskless topic: A topic created with diskless.enable=true. It has no classic prefix.
  • Pure-diskless topic: A born-diskless topic that does not have remote.storage.enable=true. Produce and fetch stay on the diskless WAL for the life of the data.
  • Consolidated diskless topic (CDT): A topic with both diskless.enable=true and remote.storage.enable=true. Producers write through the diskless WAL. A background pipeline rewrites those WAL batches into per-partition Kafka log segments and copies the closed segments to KIP-405 remote storage.
  • Consolidation frontier: The local log end offset (UnifiedLog.logEndOffset) on a replica that is materializing the WAL. Offsets below it have been written into a Kafka segment on that broker. Offsets above it still live only in the WAL.
  • WAL prune frontier: The first surviving WAL record (log_start_offset in the diskless coordinator). The pruner advances it after remote storage confirms the matching offsets.
  • Cross-tier earliest offset: The earliest offset that still exists in the whole log (remote + local + WAL). Served by ListOffsets(EARLIEST). Distinct from EARLIEST_LOCAL, which stays on the WAL prune frontier.

Compatibility, deprecation, and migration plan

Existing clusters

Turning the feature flags on is a backward-compatible upgrade. Classic topics, already-tiered classic topics, and born-diskless topics that leave remote.storage.enable off keep their current behavior, no client upgrade is required. Produce, fetch, consumer groups, and idempotent produce keep the KIP-1163 semantics. A CDT additionally behaves like a KIP-405 tiered topic for remote retention, and fetch-from-remote after local loss.

Rolling upgrade

  1. Upgrade binaries. Old brokers must not lead a consolidating partition; the controller filters them out of CDT leadership.
  2. Enable KIP-405 remote storage if it is not already on, then diskless.remote.storage.consolidation.enable. Broker config validation rejects a skip.
  3. Create new diskless topics with remote.storage.enable=true.

There is no automatic conversion of existing diskless topics. An operator who wants the old pure-WAL behavior keeps remote.storage.enable unset.

Enabling consolidation on a live diskless topic

Operator sequence:

  1. Confirm remote storage is healthy (RemoteLogManager metrics on some classic tiered topic, or a canary).
  2. kafka-configs.sh --alter ... remote.storage.enable=true.
  3. Produce and consume continue. There is no seal window.
  4. Watch ConsolidationLocalLag drop toward zero, then ConsolidationTotalLag. Remote storage begins to receive segments as local segments roll.
  5. After the pruner interval, WAL object count and coordinator batch rows should fall for the prefix that is now remote.

If consolidation needs to pause (object-storage incident, cost cap), set diskless.consolidation.fetch.rate.limit.bytes.per.second=0. Produce is unaffected. Resume by restoring the limit.

Deprecation

No existing public API is deprecated. The create-time mutual exclusion of diskless.enable and remote.storage.enable was a documented limitation of KIP-1163, not a deprecated behavior. It remains the rule when the cluster flag is off.

The feature flag stays false by default in the first release. A later KIP can flip the default once the pipeline has production time, and can decide whether new diskless topics should get remote.storage.enable=true automatically.

Rejected alternatives

Merge WAL segments

Instead of reusing Kafka's storage system we could just merge WAL segments based on some heuristic. The problem here is two-fold:

  • With this we would create a competing and incompatible long-term storage system to the classic logs.
  • Finding a good heuristic for merging WAL segments is non-trivial. These heuristics can be for example:
    • Minimum and Maximum first-generation WAL Segment lifetime (~15 mins)
    • Grouping partitions by expected expiration time bucket (~1 day)
    • Maximum WAL Segment dirty ratios (50%)
    • Minimum and Maximum WAL Segment lifetime (~30 days)
    • Target WAL Segment size (~100MB) 

Further Improvements

Better remote log metadata manager

With the current design only by plugging in RLM, a bottleneck is possible when remote logs roll over too fast. __remote_log_metadata has 50 partitions by default and every broker needs to fetch subscribe to all because partitions are scattered across all of them. This means that we need to improve the tiered storage remote log metadata management, to solve these problems:

  • limit inter-broker metadata traffic: on high frequency rollover, metadata is generated fast, which may generate inter-zone traffic, thus defeating some of the cost savings given by diskless topics.
  • better compaction: the current remote metadata log isn't compacted at all, so it can grow huge
  • improve snapshotting: tiered storage metadata has no compaction and brokers need to replay the whole log

Since the metadata manager in tiered storage is pluggable, it's possible to implement a new one without changing interfaces that is better optimized for small remote log segments.

Topic Switching

Migrating classic topics to diskless have been mentioned in previous KIPs as it is an important feature. Switching classic topics to diskless would mean that there will be an offset chosen by the leader as the swtich-over point. From this point on logs are in diskless format and before that they are in classic format but they become consolidated diskless topics, so eventually these logs move to tiered storage while keeping their log format.

Glossary

Terms from KIP-1150 and KIP-1163 keep their meaning. The following are specific to this KIP:

  • Born-diskless topic: A topic created with diskless.enable=true. It has no classic prefix.
  • Pure-diskless topic: A born-diskless topic that does not have remote.storage.enable=true. Produce and fetch stay on the diskless WAL for the life of the data.
  • Consolidated diskless topic (CDT): A topic with both diskless.enable=true and remote.storage.enable=true. Producers write through the diskless WAL. A background pipeline rewrites those WAL batches into per-partition Kafka log segments and copies the closed segments to KIP-405 remote storage.
  • Consolidation frontier: The local log end offset (UnifiedLog.logEndOffset) on a replica that is materializing the WAL. Offsets below it have been written into a Kafka segment on that broker. Offsets above it still live only in the WAL.
  • WAL prune frontier: The first surviving WAL record (log_start_offset in the diskless coordinator). The pruner advances it after remote storage confirms the matching offsets.
  • Cross-tier earliest offset: The earliest offset that still exists in the whole log (remote + local + WAL). Served by ListOffsets(EARLIEST). Distinct from EARLIEST_LOCAL, which stays on the WAL prune frontier.

Motivation

 introduces the concepts of diskless topics,  describes in detail how data is written to and read from diskless topics. KIP-1163 gives Apache Kafka a produce path that writes mixed-partition WAL objects to object storage and treats broker disks as a cache. That is the right ingest shape for high-throughput topics: one PUT covers many partitions, replication is delegated to the storage backend, and inter-zone copy of the payload goes away.

It is not a complete storage story as without a defined hand-off, three problems sit on every diskless topic for as long as it lives.

The WAL is a bad long-term log

A WAL segment is write-optimized. It packs batches from many partitions into one object so the produce path can pay one upload instead of one per partition. That is cheap to write but expensive to read: the broker has to ask the coordinator for coordinates, then reassemble a continuous per-partition stream from interleaved objects.

That cost is acceptable for the tail, where the produce cache is hot and most consumers sit but it is the wrong shape for everything else:

  • A lagging consumer walks coordinator metadata and issues ranged GETs against objects that also contain partitions it does not want.
  • The coordinator's batch-coordinate tables grow with every produce for the life of the topic.

Kafka already has a backend for inactive data

Several subsystems assume Kafka log segments:

  • RemoteLogManager copies closed local segments to remote storage and expires them by retention.ms / retention.bytes.
  • LeaderEpochFileCache and the KIP-405 tier-state machine rebuild a replica from remote storage after local loss.
  • Local retention (local.retention.ms / local.retention.bytes) evicts broker-local segments once remote storage has them.
  • Existing RSM and RLMM plugins, remote-fetch paths, and tools that inspect segment files all speak that format.

Therefore transforming WAL segments into classic Kafka format would ensure compatibility with existing systems while providing good produce and consume characteristics.

Physical deletion cannot meet a deadline

KIP-1163 already called this out under batch deletion. A logically deleted batch still occupies a WAL object kept alive by other partitions. Compliance rules that demand physical deletion by a deadline cannot be met until every other live batch in that object is gone, or until the batch is copied into a per-partition object that can be deleted on its own clock. Moving data into KIP-405 segments bounds WAL object lifetime by how long consolidation takes to catch the tail, not by the slowest partition sharing the object. After the copy, remote retention is the ordinary KIP-405 policy.

Proposed changes

High level architecture

Diskless topics should have leaders as leadership and followers give locality and caching. If every broker is a replica, interconnectedness is high and the cache is inefficient and in the worst case every broker caches the same replica. A single replica is the other extreme as it can work in a small single-region or on-prem install, but fetching from the leader then incurs extra cross-region cost.

This shape matches the Kafka replica-fetcher model that we'd use for implementing diskless object consolidation. A leader replica would handle produce and consume traffic while replication would be done by followers which fetch WAL data from the broker local cache or pull directly from the object storage. The followers would also serve consume traffic (follower fetch). Interconnectedness in this case would stay relatively low and cross-region traffic could be avoided which would make caching more efficient because a local cached segment (a classic Kafka segment) would live only where it is read.

Consolidation pipeline

Without consolidation, diskless WAL segments are stored in object storage where they remain until log.local.retention.ms elapses, then the broker deletes them. With consolidation, a fetcher would read the oldest batches from the diskless WAL, in insertion order so ordering is preserved, and would append them to a per-partition UnifiedLog through the Partition class. The RemoteLogManager would copy those local segments to remote storage the same way it does for a classic tiered topic. After remote storage confirms a batch, the pruner would delete the matching WAL data.

The fetcher splits interleaved WAL files into per-partition local segments. The RemoteLogManager then tiers those segments to remote storage.

Log continuity

In Kafka tiered storage, tiered and local offsets can overlap, as KIP-405 defines. The split between diskless and classic local offsets is similar as diskless offsets overlap local offsets because the local log is a cache, not persistent storage. Depending on the cleanup schedule, diskless logs may totally overlap local logs and even reach deeper into the tiered offset range. That happens when older segments still hold data that has not been migrated to remote storage, so the broker cannot delete it yet. That overlap is expected, the broker cleans up diskless segments periodically as it consolidates them.

Read path

With consolidation, the broker can serve a consumer fetch from three sources:

  • Tiered offset space: Classic log segments on remote storage ([0, highestOffsetInRemoteStorage]).
  • Diskless offset space: WAL segments on remote storage.
  • WAL cache: A local in-broker cache (a subset of the diskless offset space).

ReplicaManager.fetchMessages routes a consolidating partition as follows:

  • If the fetch offset falls in the tiered range (below localLogStartOffset), the broker routes the request to the RemoteLogManager, as it does for any tiered topic.
  • If the fetch offset is inside the local log, the broker reads the local log. If that read doesn't satisfy minBytes, the broker supplements with a synchronous diskless fetch starting at the local log end offset and merges the two through ConcatenatedRecords.concat. The supplement avoids parking the consumer in the delayed-fetch purgatory at the local/diskless boundary when diskless data is already available.
  • If the fetch offset is at or beyond the local log end offset, the broker serves the request from the diskless subsystem (cache or object storage). Since most of the time these will be relatively fresh, they have a high chance of being cached in the broker and object storage access should be rare.

If every partition in the request is consolidating, the broker applies the supplement inline and returns the response immediately. If the request mixes consolidating and pure-diskless partitions, the supplement and the diskless fetch run concurrently in DelayedFetch.onComplete, so latency is the slower of the two, not their sum.

WAL pruning

The process of removing data that has been consolidated is called pruning. This entails the deletion of the batch coordinate from the coordinator. It doesn't involve deleting WAL objects from object storage as they may contain data that haven't been consolidated yet. In a timely manner they should be consolidated and a background process should remove those objects that don't have any batch data.

Remote reads after WAL prune

After a batch is consolidated to remote storage and the WAL is pruned, data below the diskless WAL start lives only in the remote tier. If a fetch targets an offset in [logStartOffset, disklessWALStart)  DisklessLeaderEndPoint.fetch signals OFFSET_MOVED_TO_TIERED_STORAGE and clears the records. The stock Kafka tier-state machine then rebuilds the leader-epoch cache and producer snapshot from remote storage before it resumes the WAL fetch. Some examples for this scenario could be fetch after local-log loss, or a follower catching up.

This is the read-from-remote path that lets a consolidated topic survive losing every local copy. 

Cross-tier log start

For implementing proper fetch routing, the followers need to know what is the earliest offset across log types. This is what cross-tier log start means. In case of plain Kafka logs, reclaiming expired logs is simple. LogManager runs UnifiedLog.deleteOldSegments() on log.retention.check.interval.ms (default 5 minutes). For cleanup.policy=delete it deletes closed local segments that breach time or size retentions. Followers learn about it by the fetch response and advance their start offset and delete local segments below it. Tiered storage is a bit more complicated but follows the same logic. RemoteLogManager on the leader expires remote segments, then increment the log start offset. Followers then learn about this the same way: through the fetch response.

With the planned model of consolidation fetchers that fetch from WAL, there is no way to communicate this through the fetch response as it doesn't fetch the leader. Instead of this, when the leader advances the cross-tier log start (DeleteRecords or retention enforcement), it stores it in the coordinator. This will be fetched by the followers whenever a ListOffsets(EARLIEST) is issued to them. It can also be cached for efficiency, so an OFFSET_OUT_OF_RANGE error would trigger the refresh of the follower entry to avoid pinging the coordinator too often. The followers issue DisklessListOffsets to fetch the cross-tier log start from the leaders.

Compatibility, deprecation, and migration plan

Existing clusters

Turning the feature flags on is a backward-compatible upgrade. Classic topics, already-tiered classic topics, and born-diskless topics that leave remote.storage.enable off keep their current behavior, no client upgrade is required. Produce, fetch, consumer groups, and idempotent produce keep the KIP-1163 semantics. A CDT additionally behaves like a KIP-405 tiered topic for remote retention, and fetch-from-remote after local loss.

Rolling upgrade

  1. Upgrade binaries. Old brokers must not lead a consolidating partition; the controller filters them out of CDT leadership.
  2. Enable KIP-405 remote storage if it is not already on, then diskless.remote.storage.consolidation.enable. Broker config validation rejects a skip.
  3. Create new diskless topics with remote.storage.enable=true.

There is no automatic conversion of existing diskless topics. An operator who wants the old pure-WAL behavior keeps remote.storage.enable unset.

Enabling consolidation on a live diskless topic

Operator sequence:

  1. Confirm remote storage is healthy (RemoteLogManager metrics on some classic tiered topic, or a canary).
  2. kafka-configs.sh --alter ... remote.storage.enable=true.
  3. Produce and consume continue.
  4. Watch ConsolidationLocalLag drop toward zero, then ConsolidationTotalLag. Remote storage begins to receive segments as local segments roll.
  5. After the pruner interval, WAL object count and coordinator batch rows should fall for the prefix that is now remote.

If consolidation needs to pause (object-storage incident, cost cap), set diskless.consolidation.fetch.rate.limit.bytes.per.second=0. Produce is unaffected. Resume by restoring the limit.

Deprecation

No existing public API is deprecated. The create-time mutual exclusion of diskless.enable and remote.storage.enable was a documented limitation of KIP-1163, not a deprecated behavior. It remains the rule when the cluster flag is off.

The feature flag stays false by default in the first release. A later KIP can flip the default once the pipeline has production time, and can decide whether new diskless topics should get remote.storage.enable=true automatically.

Rejected alternatives

Merge WAL segments

Instead of reusing Kafka's storage system we could just merge WAL segments based on some heuristic. The problem here is two-fold:

  • We would create a competing and incompatible long-term storage system to the classic logs.
  • Finding a good heuristic for merging WAL segments is non-trivial and there can be many implementations that could make it hard for users to choose from. These heuristics can be for example:
    • Minimum and Maximum first-generation WAL Segment lifetime (~15 mins)
    • Grouping partitions by expected expiration time bucket (~1 day)
    • Maximum WAL Segment dirty ratios (50%)
    • Minimum and Maximum WAL Segment lifetime (~30 days)
    • Target WAL Segment size (~100MB)

Further Improvements

Better remote log metadata manager

With the current design only by plugging in RLM, a bottleneck is possible when remote logs roll over too fast. __remote_log_metadata has 50 partitions by default and every broker needs to fetch subscribe to all because partitions are scattered across all of them. This means that we need to improve the tiered storage remote log metadata management, to solve these problems:

  • limit inter-broker metadata traffic: on high frequency rollover, metadata is generated fast, which may generate inter-zone traffic, thus defeating some of the cost savings given by diskless topics.
  • better compaction: the current remote metadata log isn't compacted at all, so it can grow huge
  • improve snapshotting: tiered storage metadata has no compaction and brokers need to replay the whole log

Since the metadata manager in tiered storage is pluggable, it's possible to implement a new one without changing interfaces that is better optimized for small remote log segments.

Topic Switching

Migrating classic topics to diskless have been mentioned in previous KIPs as it is an important feature. Switching classic topics to diskless would mean that there will be an offset chosen by the leader as the swtich-over point. From this point on logs are in diskless format and before that they are in classic format but they become consolidated diskless topics, so eventually these logs move to tiered storage while keeping their log format.

Glossary

Terms from KIP-1150 and KIP-1163 keep their meaning. The following are specific to this KIP:

  • Born-diskless topic: A topic created with diskless.enable=true. It has no classic prefix.
  • Pure-diskless topic: A born-diskless topic that does not have remote.storage.enable=true. Produce and fetch stay on the diskless WAL for the life of the data.
  • Consolidated diskless topic (CDT): A topic with both diskless.enable=true and remote.storage.enable=true. Producers write through the diskless WAL. A background pipeline rewrites those WAL batches into per-partition Kafka log segments and copies the closed segments to KIP-405 remote storage.
  • Consolidation frontier: The local log end offset (UnifiedLog.logEndOffset) on a replica that is materializing the WAL. Offsets below it have been written into a Kafka segment on that broker. Offsets above it still live only in the WAL.
  • WAL prune frontier: The first surviving WAL record (log_start_offset in the diskless coordinator). The pruner advances it after remote storage confirms the matching offsets.
  • Cross-tier earliest offset: The earliest offset that still exists in the whole log (remote + local + WAL). Served by ListOffsets(EARLIEST). Distinct from EARLIEST_LOCAL, which stays on the WAL prune frontier.

Motivation

 introduces the concepts of diskless topics,  describes in detail how data is written to and read from diskless topics. KIP-1163 gives Apache Kafka a produce path that writes mixed-partition WAL objects to object storage and treats broker disks as a cache. That is the right ingest shape for high-throughput topics: one PUT covers many partitions, replication is delegated to the storage backend, and inter-zone copy of the payload goes away.

It is not a complete storage story as without a defined hand-off, three problems sit on every diskless topic for as long as it lives.

The WAL is a bad long-term log

A WAL segment is write-optimized. It packs batches from many partitions into one object so the produce path can pay one upload instead of one per partition. That is cheap to write but expensive to read: the broker has to ask the coordinator for coordinates, then reassemble a continuous per-partition stream from interleaved objects.

That cost is acceptable for the tail, where the produce cache is hot and most consumers sit but it is the wrong shape for everything else:

  • A lagging consumer walks coordinator metadata and issues ranged GETs against objects that also contain partitions it does not want.
  • The coordinator's batch-coordinate tables grow with every produce for the life of the topic.

Kafka already has a backend for inactive data

Several subsystems assume Kafka log segments:

  • RemoteLogManager copies closed local segments to remote storage and expires them by retention.ms / retention.bytes.
  • LeaderEpochFileCache and the KIP-405 tier-state machine rebuild a replica from remote storage after local loss.
  • Local retention (local.retention.ms / local.retention.bytes) evicts broker-local segments once remote storage has them.
  • Existing RSM and RLMM plugins, remote-fetch paths, and tools that inspect segment files all speak that format.

Therefore transforming WAL segments into classic Kafka format would ensure compatibility with existing systems while providing good produce and consume characteristics.

Physical deletion cannot meet a deadline

KIP-1163 already called this out under batch deletion. A logically deleted batch still occupies a WAL object kept alive by other partitions. Compliance rules that demand physical deletion by a deadline cannot be met until every other live batch in that object is gone, or until the batch is copied into a per-partition object that can be deleted on its own clock. Moving data into KIP-405 segments bounds WAL object lifetime by how long consolidation takes to catch the tail, not by the slowest partition sharing the object. After the copy, remote retention is the ordinary KIP-405 policy.

Proposed changes

High level architecture

Diskless topics should have leaders as leadership and followers give locality and caching. If every broker is a replica, interconnectedness is high and the cache is inefficient and in the worst case every broker caches the same replica. A single replica is the other extreme as it can work in a small single-region or on-prem install, but fetching from the leader then incurs extra cross-region cost.

This shape matches the Kafka replica-fetcher model that we'd use for implementing diskless object consolidation. A leader replica would handle produce and consume traffic while replication would be done by followers which fetch WAL data from the broker local cache or pull directly from the object storage. The followers would also serve consume traffic (follower fetch). Interconnectedness in this case would stay relatively low and cross-region traffic could be avoided which would make caching more efficient because a local cached segment (a classic Kafka segment) would live only where it is read.

Consolidation pipeline

Without consolidation, diskless WAL segments are stored in object storage where they remain until log.local.retention.ms elapses, then the broker deletes them. With consolidation, a fetcher would read the oldest batches from the diskless WAL, in insertion order so ordering is preserved, and would append them to a per-partition UnifiedLog through the Partition class. The RemoteLogManager would copy those local segments to remote storage the same way it does for a classic tiered topic. After remote storage confirms a batch, the pruner would delete the matching WAL data.

The fetcher splits interleaved WAL files into per-partition local segments. The RemoteLogManager then tiers those segments to remote storage.

Log continuity

In Kafka tiered storage, tiered and local offsets can overlap, as KIP-405 defines. The split between diskless and classic local offsets is similar as diskless offsets overlap local offsets because the local log is a cache, not persistent storage. Depending on the cleanup schedule, diskless logs may totally overlap local logs and even reach deeper into the tiered offset range. That happens when older segments still hold data that has not been migrated to remote storage, so the broker cannot delete it yet. That overlap is expected, the broker cleans up diskless segments periodically as it consolidates them.

Read path

With consolidation, the broker can serve a consumer fetch from three sources:

  • Tiered offset space: Classic log segments on remote storage ([0, highestOffsetInRemoteStorage]).
  • Diskless offset space: WAL segments on remote storage.
  • WAL cache: A local in-broker cache (a subset of the diskless offset space).

ReplicaManager.fetchMessages routes a consolidating partition as follows:

  • If the fetch offset falls in the tiered range (below localLogStartOffset), the broker routes the request to the RemoteLogManager, as it does for any tiered topic.
  • If the fetch offset is inside the local log, the broker reads the local log. If that read doesn't satisfy minBytes, the broker supplements with a synchronous diskless fetch starting at the local log end offset and merges the two through ConcatenatedRecords.concat. The supplement avoids parking the consumer in the delayed-fetch purgatory at the local/diskless boundary when diskless data is already available.
  • If the fetch offset is at or beyond the local log end offset, the broker serves the request from the diskless subsystem (cache or object storage). Since most of the time these will be relatively fresh, they have a high chance of being cached in the broker and object storage access should be rare.

If every partition in the request is consolidating, the broker applies the supplement inline and returns the response immediately. If the request mixes consolidating and pure-diskless partitions, the supplement and the diskless fetch run concurrently in DelayedFetch.onComplete, so latency is the slower of the two, not their sum.

WAL pruning

The process of removing data that has been consolidated is called pruning. This entails the deletion of the batch coordinate from the coordinator. It doesn't involve deleting WAL objects from object storage as they may contain data that haven't been consolidated yet. In a timely manner they should be consolidated and a background process should remove those objects that don't have any batch data.

Remote reads after WAL prune

After a batch is consolidated to remote storage and the WAL is pruned, data below the diskless WAL start lives only in the remote tier. If a fetch targets an offset in [logStartOffset, disklessWALStart)  DisklessLeaderEndPoint.fetch signals OFFSET_MOVED_TO_TIERED_STORAGE and clears the records. The stock Kafka tier-state machine then rebuilds the leader-epoch cache and producer snapshot from remote storage before it resumes the WAL fetch. Some examples for this scenario could be fetch after local-log loss, or a follower catching up.

This is the read-from-remote path that lets a consolidated topic survive losing every local copy. 

Cross-tier log start

For implementing proper fetch routing, the followers need to know what is the earliest offset across log types. This is what cross-tier log start means. In case of plain Kafka logs, reclaiming expired logs is simple. LogManager runs UnifiedLog.deleteOldSegments() on log.retention.check.interval.ms (default 5 minutes). For cleanup.policy=delete it deletes closed local segments that breach time or size retentions. Followers learn about it by the fetch response and advance their start offset and delete local segments below it. Tiered storage is a bit more complicated but follows the same logic. RemoteLogManager on the leader expires remote segments, then increment the log start offset. Followers then learn about this the same way: through the fetch response.

With the planned model of consolidation fetchers that fetch from WAL, there is no way to communicate this through the fetch response as it doesn't fetch the leader. Instead of this, when the leader advances the cross-tier log start (DeleteRecords or retention enforcement), it stores it in the coordinator. It can also be cached for efficiency on the followers, where an OFFSET_OUT_OF_RANGE error would trigger the refresh of the follower entry to avoid pinging the coordinator too often. The followers issue DisklessListOffsets to fetch the cross-tier log start from the coordinator.

  • limit inter-broker metadata traffic: on high frequency rollover, metadata is generated fast, which may generate inter-zone traffic, thus defeating some of the cost savings given by diskless topics.
  • better compaction: the current remote metadata log isn't compacted at all, so it can grow huge

Glossary

Terms from KIP-1150 and KIP-1163 keep their meaning. The following are specific to this KIP:

  • Born-diskless topic: A topic created with diskless.enable=true. It has no classic prefix.
  • Pure-diskless topic: A born-diskless topic that does not have remote.storage.enable=true. Produce and fetch stay on the diskless WAL for the life of the data.
  • Consolidated diskless topic (CDT): A topic with both diskless.enable=true and remote.storage.enable=true. Producers write through the diskless WAL. A background pipeline rewrites those WAL batches into per-partition Kafka log segments and copies the closed segments to KIP-405 remote storage.
  • Consolidation frontier: The local log end offset (UnifiedLog.logEndOffset) on a replica that is materializing the WAL. Offsets below it have been written into a Kafka segment on that broker. Offsets above it still live only in the WAL.
  • WAL prune frontier: The first surviving WAL record (log_start_offset in the diskless coordinator). The pruner advances it after remote storage confirms the matching offsets.
  • Cross-tier earliest offset: The earliest offset that still exists in the whole log (remote + local + WAL). Served by ListOffsets(EARLIEST). Distinct from EARLIEST_LOCAL, which stays on the WAL prune frontier.

Motivation

 introduces the concepts of diskless topics,  describes in detail how data is written to and read from diskless topics. KIP-1163 gives Apache Kafka a produce path that writes mixed-partition WAL objects to object storage and treats broker disks as a cache. That is the right ingest shape for high-throughput topics: one PUT covers many partitions, replication is delegated to the storage backend, and inter-zone copy of the payload goes away.

It is not a complete storage story as without a defined hand-off, three problems sit on every diskless topic for as long as it lives.

The WAL is a bad long-term log

A WAL segment is write-optimized. It packs batches from many partitions into one object so the produce path can pay one upload instead of one per partition. That is cheap to write but expensive to read: the broker has to ask the coordinator for coordinates, then reassemble a continuous per-partition stream from interleaved objects.

That cost is acceptable for the tail, where the produce cache is hot and most consumers sit but it is the wrong shape for everything else:

  • A lagging consumer walks coordinator metadata and issues ranged GETs against objects that also contain partitions it does not want.
  • The coordinator's batch-coordinate tables grow with every produce for the life of the topic.

Kafka already has a backend for inactive data

Several subsystems assume Kafka log segments:

  • RemoteLogManager copies closed local segments to remote storage and expires them by retention.ms / retention.bytes.
  • LeaderEpochFileCache and the KIP-405 tier-state machine rebuild a replica from remote storage after local loss.
  • Local retention (local.retention.ms / local.retention.bytes) evicts broker-local segments once remote storage has them.
  • Existing RSM and RLMM plugins, remote-fetch paths, and tools that inspect segment files all speak that format.

Therefore transforming WAL segments into classic Kafka format would ensure compatibility with existing systems while providing good produce and consume characteristics.

Physical deletion cannot meet a deadline

KIP-1163 already called this out under batch deletion. A logically deleted batch still occupies a WAL object kept alive by other partitions. Compliance rules that demand physical deletion by a deadline cannot be met until every other live batch in that object is gone, or until the batch is copied into a per-partition object that can be deleted on its own clock. Moving data into KIP-405 segments bounds WAL object lifetime by how long consolidation takes to catch the tail, not by the slowest partition sharing the object. After the copy, remote retention is the ordinary KIP-405 policy.

Proposed changes

High level architecture

Diskless topics should have leaders as leadership and followers give locality and caching. If every broker is a replica, interconnectedness is high and the cache is inefficient and in the worst case every broker caches the same replica. A single replica is the other extreme as it can work in a small single-region or on-prem install, but fetching from the leader then incurs extra cross-region cost.

This shape matches the Kafka replica-fetcher model that we'd use for implementing diskless object consolidation. A leader replica would handle produce and consume traffic while replication would be done by followers which fetch WAL data from the broker local cache or pull directly from the object storage. The followers would also serve consume traffic (follower fetch). Interconnectedness in this case would stay relatively low and cross-region traffic could be avoided which would make caching more efficient because a local cached segment (a classic Kafka segment) would live only where it is read.

Consolidation pipeline

Without consolidation, diskless WAL segments are stored in object storage where they remain until log.local.retention.ms elapses, then the broker deletes them. With consolidation, a fetcher would read the oldest batches from the diskless WAL, in insertion order so ordering is preserved, and would append them to a per-partition UnifiedLog through the Partition class. The RemoteLogManager would copy those local segments to remote storage the same way it does for a classic tiered topic. After remote storage confirms a batch, the pruner would delete the matching WAL data.

The fetcher splits interleaved WAL files into per-partition local segments. The RemoteLogManager then tiers those segments to remote storage.

Log continuity

In Kafka tiered storage, tiered and local offsets can overlap, as KIP-405 defines. The split between diskless and classic local offsets is similar as diskless offsets overlap local offsets because the local log is a cache, not persistent storage. Depending on the cleanup schedule, diskless logs may totally overlap local logs and even reach deeper into the tiered offset range. That happens when older segments still hold data that has not been migrated to remote storage, so the broker cannot delete it yet. That overlap is expected, the broker cleans up diskless segments periodically as it consolidates them.

Read path

With consolidation, the broker can serve a consumer fetch from three sources:

  • Tiered offset space: Classic log segments on remote storage ([0, highestOffsetInRemoteStorage]).
  • Diskless offset space: WAL segments on remote storage.
  • WAL cache: A local in-broker cache (a subset of the diskless offset space).

ReplicaManager.fetchMessages routes a consolidating partition as follows:

  • If the fetch offset falls in the tiered range (below localLogStartOffset), the broker routes the request to the RemoteLogManager, as it does for any tiered topic.
  • If the fetch offset is inside the local log, the broker reads the local log. If that read doesn't satisfy minBytes, the broker supplements with a synchronous diskless fetch starting at the local log end offset and merges the two through ConcatenatedRecords.concat. The supplement avoids parking the consumer in the delayed-fetch purgatory at the local/diskless boundary when diskless data is already available.
  • If the fetch offset is at or beyond the local log end offset, the broker serves the request from the diskless subsystem (cache or object storage). Since most of the time these will be relatively fresh, they have a high chance of being cached in the broker and object storage access should be rare.

If every partition in the request is consolidating, the broker applies the supplement inline and returns the response immediately. If the request mixes consolidating and pure-diskless partitions, the supplement and the diskless fetch run concurrently in DelayedFetch.onComplete, so latency is the slower of the two, not their sum.

WAL pruning

The process of removing data that has been consolidated is called pruning. This entails the deletion of the batch coordinate from the coordinator. It doesn't involve deleting WAL objects from object storage as they may contain data that haven't been consolidated yet. In a timely manner they should be consolidated and a background process should remove those objects that don't have any batch data.

Remote reads after WAL prune

After a batch is consolidated to remote storage and the WAL is pruned, data below the diskless WAL start lives only in the remote tier. If a fetch targets an offset in [logStartOffset, disklessWALStart)  DisklessLeaderEndPoint.fetch signals OFFSET_MOVED_TO_TIERED_STORAGE and clears the records. The stock Kafka tier-state machine then rebuilds the leader-epoch cache and producer snapshot from remote storage before it resumes the WAL fetch. Some examples for this scenario could be fetch after local-log loss, or a follower catching up.

This is the read-from-remote path that lets a consolidated topic survive losing every local copy. 

Cross-tier log start

For implementing proper fetch routing, the followers need to know what is the earliest offset across log types. This is what cross-tier log start means. In case of plain Kafka logs, reclaiming expired logs is simple. LogManager runs UnifiedLog.deleteOldSegments() on log.retention.check.interval.ms (default 5 minutes). For cleanup.policy=delete it deletes closed local segments that breach time or size retentions. Followers learn about it by the fetch response and advance their start offset and delete local segments below it. Tiered storage is a bit more complicated but follows the same logic. RemoteLogManager on the leader expires remote segments, then increment the log start offset. Followers then learn about this the same way: through the fetch response.

With the planned model of consolidation fetchers that fetch from WAL, there is no way to communicate this through the fetch response as it doesn't fetch the leader. Instead of this, when the leader advances the cross-tier log start (DeleteRecords or retention enforcement), it stores it in the coordinator. It can also be cached for efficiency on the followers, where an OFFSET_OUT_OF_RANGE error would trigger the refresh of the follower entry to avoid pinging the coordinator too often. The followers issue DisklessListOffsets to fetch the cross-tier log start from the coordinator.

Turning the feature flags on is a backward-compatible upgrade. Rolling upgrade

  1. Upgrade binaries. Old brokers must not lead a consolidating partition; the controller filters them out of CDT leadership.

Glossary

Terms from KIP-1150 and KIP-1163 keep their meaning. The following are specific to this KIP:

  • Born-diskless topic: A topic created with diskless.enable=true. It has no classic prefix.
  • Pure-diskless topic: A born-diskless topic that isn't capable for diskless consolidation. Produce and fetch stay on the diskless WAL for the life of the data.
  • Consolidated diskless topic (CDT): A topic with both diskless.enable=true. Producers write through the diskless WAL. A background pipeline rewrites those WAL batches into per-partition Kafka log segments and copies the closed segments to KIP-405 remote storage.
  • Consolidation frontier: The local log end offset (UnifiedLog.logEndOffset) on a replica that is materializing the WAL. Offsets below it have been written into a Kafka segment on that broker. Offsets above it still live only in the WAL.
  • WAL prune frontier: The first surviving WAL record (log_start_offset in the diskless coordinator). The pruner advances it after remote storage confirms the matching offsets.
  • Cross-tier earliest offset: The earliest offset that still exists in the whole log (remote + local + WAL). Served by ListOffsets(EARLIEST). Distinct from EARLIEST_LOCAL, which stays on the WAL prune frontier.

Motivation

 introduces the concepts of diskless topics,  describes in detail how data is written to and read from diskless topics. KIP-1163 gives Apache Kafka a produce path that writes mixed-partition WAL objects to object storage and treats broker disks as a cache. That is the right ingest shape for high-throughput topics: one PUT covers many partitions, replication is delegated to the storage backend, and inter-zone copy of the payload goes away.

It is not a complete storage story as without a defined hand-off, three problems sit on every diskless topic for as long as it lives.

The WAL is a bad long-term log

A WAL segment is write-optimized. It packs batches from many partitions into one object so the produce path can pay one upload instead of one per partition. That is cheap to write but expensive to read: the broker has to ask the coordinator for coordinates, then reassemble a continuous per-partition stream from interleaved objects.

That cost is acceptable for the tail, where the produce cache is hot and most consumers sit but it is the wrong shape for everything else:

  • A lagging consumer walks coordinator metadata and issues ranged GETs against objects that also contain partitions it does not want.
  • The coordinator's batch-coordinate tables grow with every produce for the life of the topic.

Kafka already has a backend for inactive data

Several subsystems assume Kafka log segments:

  • RemoteLogManager copies closed local segments to remote storage and expires them by retention.ms / retention.bytes.
  • LeaderEpochFileCache and the KIP-405 tier-state machine rebuild a replica from remote storage after local loss.
  • Local retention (local.retention.ms / local.retention.bytes) evicts broker-local segments once remote storage has them.
  • Existing RSM and RLMM plugins, remote-fetch paths, and tools that inspect segment files all speak that format.

Therefore transforming WAL segments into classic Kafka format would ensure compatibility with existing systems while providing good produce and consume characteristics.

Physical deletion cannot meet a deadline

KIP-1163 already called this out under batch deletion. A logically deleted batch still occupies a WAL object kept alive by other partitions. Compliance rules that demand physical deletion by a deadline cannot be met until every other live batch in that object is gone, or until the batch is copied into a per-partition object that can be deleted on its own clock. Moving data into KIP-405 segments bounds WAL object lifetime by how long consolidation takes to catch the tail, not by the slowest partition sharing the object. After the copy, remote retention is the ordinary KIP-405 policy.

Proposed changes

High level architecture

Diskless topics should have leaders as leadership and followers give locality and caching. If every broker is a replica, interconnectedness is high and the cache is inefficient and in the worst case every broker caches the same replica. A single replica is the other extreme as it can work in a small single-region or on-prem install, but fetching from the leader then incurs extra cross-region cost.

This shape matches the Kafka replica-fetcher model that we'd use for implementing diskless object consolidation. A leader replica would handle produce and consume traffic while replication would be done by followers which fetch WAL data from the broker local cache or pull directly from the object storage. The followers would also serve consume traffic (follower fetch). Interconnectedness in this case would stay relatively low and cross-region traffic could be avoided which would make caching more efficient because a local cached segment (a classic Kafka segment) would live only where it is read.

Consolidation pipeline

Without consolidation, diskless WAL segments are stored in object storage where they remain until log.local.retention.ms elapses, then the broker deletes them. With consolidation, a fetcher would read the oldest batches from the diskless WAL, in insertion order so ordering is preserved, and would append them to a per-partition UnifiedLog through the Partition class. The RemoteLogManager would copy those local segments to remote storage the same way it does for a classic tiered topic. After remote storage confirms a batch, the pruner would delete the matching WAL data.

The fetcher splits interleaved WAL files into per-partition local segments. The RemoteLogManager then tiers those segments to remote storage.

Log continuity

In Kafka tiered storage, tiered and local offsets can overlap, as KIP-405 defines. The split between diskless and classic local offsets is similar as diskless offsets overlap local offsets because the local log is a cache, not persistent storage. Depending on the cleanup schedule, diskless logs may totally overlap local logs and even reach deeper into the tiered offset range. That happens when older segments still hold data that has not been migrated to remote storage, so the broker cannot delete it yet. That overlap is expected, the broker cleans up diskless segments periodically as it consolidates them.

Read path

With consolidation, the broker can serve a consumer fetch from three sources:

  • Tiered offset space: Classic log segments on remote storage ([0, highestOffsetInRemoteStorage]).
  • Diskless offset space: WAL segments on remote storage.
  • WAL cache: A local in-broker cache (a subset of the diskless offset space).

ReplicaManager.fetchMessages routes a consolidating partition as follows:

  • If the fetch offset falls in the tiered range (below localLogStartOffset), the broker routes the request to the RemoteLogManager, as it does for any tiered topic.
  • If the fetch offset is inside the local log, the broker reads the local log. If that read doesn't satisfy minBytes, the broker supplements with a synchronous diskless fetch starting at the local log end offset and merges the two through ConcatenatedRecords.concat. The supplement avoids parking the consumer in the delayed-fetch purgatory at the local/diskless boundary when diskless data is already available.
  • If the fetch offset is at or beyond the local log end offset, the broker serves the request from the diskless subsystem (cache or object storage). Since most of the time these will be relatively fresh, they have a high chance of being cached in the broker and object storage access should be rare.

If every partition in the request is consolidating, the broker applies the supplement inline and returns the response immediately.

WAL pruning

The process of removing data that has been consolidated is called pruning. This entails the deletion of the batch coordinate from the coordinator. It doesn't involve deleting WAL objects from object storage as they may contain data that haven't been consolidated yet. In a timely manner they should be consolidated and a background process should remove those objects that don't have any batch data.

Remote reads after WAL prune

After a batch is consolidated to remote storage and the WAL is pruned, data below the diskless WAL start lives only in the remote tier. If a fetch targets an offset in [logStartOffset, disklessWALStart)  DisklessLeaderEndPoint.fetch signals OFFSET_MOVED_TO_TIERED_STORAGE and clears the records. The stock Kafka tier-state machine then rebuilds the leader-epoch cache and producer snapshot from remote storage before it resumes the WAL fetch. Some examples for this scenario could be fetch after local-log loss, or a follower catching up.

This is the read-from-remote path that lets a consolidated topic survive losing every local copy. 

Cross-tier log start

For implementing proper fetch routing, the followers need to know what is the earliest offset across log types. This is what cross-tier log start means. In case of plain Kafka logs, reclaiming expired logs is simple. LogManager runs UnifiedLog.deleteOldSegments() on log.retention.check.interval.ms (default 5 minutes). For cleanup.policy=delete it deletes closed local segments that breach time or size retentions. Followers learn about it by the fetch response and advance their start offset and delete local segments below it. Tiered storage is a bit more complicated but follows the same logic. RemoteLogManager on the leader expires remote segments, then increment the log start offset. Followers then learn about this the same way: through the fetch response.

With the planned model of consolidation fetchers that fetch from WAL, there is no way to communicate this through the fetch response as it doesn't fetch the leader. Instead of this, when the leader advances the cross-tier log start (DeleteRecords or retention enforcement), it stores it in the coordinator. It can also be cached for efficiency on the followers, where an OFFSET_OUT_OF_RANGE error would trigger the refresh of the follower entry to avoid pinging the coordinator too often. The followers issue DisklessListOffsets to fetch the cross-tier log start from the coordinator.

Public interfaces

No existing Produce, Fetch, or consumer-group request schema changes. Clients keep the same requests. A CDT is semantically a Kafka topic with KIP-405 remote storage in front of a diskless produce path.

Network protocol

No new client API keys. No new fields on Produce, Fetch, Metadata, or ListOffsets.

OFFSET_MOVED_TO_TIERED_STORAGE (already used by KIP-405 follower fetch) is also used on the consolidation fetch path when the requested offset sits below the WAL prune frontier. Clients do not see a new error on the ordinary consume path: the broker either serves the data from remote storage or translates the condition into the existing fetch-from-remote flow.

Diskless coordinator

KIP-1164 remains the coordinator KIP. It already defers "offloading to tiered storage" to a later KIP. This KIP adds that piece: two mutating coordinator RPCs, two metadata records on __diskless_metadata, and a behavior change on the existing DisklessListOffsets path.

These are broker-to-coordinator calls (CLUSTER_ACTION), not client APIs. They follow the KIP-1164 model: the metadata topic is the source of truth; the coordinator leader appends records and materializes them into local state (SQLite, in KIP-1164). This KIP does not add a second store and does not prescribe how that local state is laid out.

Compatibility, deprecation, and migration plan

Existing clusters

Turning the feature flags on is a backward-compatible upgrade. Classic topics and already-tiered classic topics keep their current behavior, no client upgrade is required. Produce, fetch, consumer groups, and idempotent produce keep the KIP-1163 semantics. A CDT additionally behaves like a KIP-405 tiered topic for remote retention, and fetch-from-remote after local loss.

Enabling consolidation on a live diskless topic

Operator sequence:

  1. Confirm remote storage is healthy (RemoteLogManager metrics on some classic tiered topic, or a canary).
  2. kafka-configs.sh --alter ... diskless.enable=true.
  3. Produce and consume continue.
  4. Watch ConsolidationLocalLag drop toward zero, then ConsolidationTotalLag. Remote storage begins to receive segments as local segments roll.
  5. After the pruner interval, WAL object count and coordinator batch rows should fall for the prefix that is now remote.

If consolidation needs to pause (object-storage incident, cost cap), set diskless.consolidation.fetch.rate.limit.bytes.per.second=0. Produce is unaffected. Resume by restoring the limit.

Rejected alternatives

Merge WAL segments

Instead of reusing Kafka's storage system we could just merge WAL segments based on some heuristic. The problem here is two-fold:

  • We would create a competing and incompatible long-term storage system to the classic logs.
  • Finding a good heuristic for merging WAL segments is non-trivial and there can be many implementations that could make it hard for users to choose from. These heuristics can be for example:
    • Minimum and Maximum first-generation WAL Segment lifetime (~15 mins)
    • Grouping partitions by expected expiration time bucket (~1 day)
    • Maximum WAL Segment dirty ratios (50%)
    • Minimum and Maximum WAL Segment lifetime (~30 days)
    • Target WAL Segment size (~100MB)

Further Improvements

Better remote log metadata manager

With the current design only by plugging in RLM, a bottleneck is possible when remote logs roll over too fast. __remote_log_metadata has 50 partitions by default and every broker needs to fetch subscribe to all because partitions are scattered across all of them. This means that we need to improve the tiered storage remote log metadata management, to solve these problems:

  • limit inter-broker metadata traffic: on high frequency rollover, metadata is generated fast, which may generate inter-zone traffic, thus defeating some of the cost savings given by diskless topics.
  • better compaction: the current remote metadata log isn't compacted at all, so it can grow huge
  • improve snapshotting: tiered storage metadata has no compaction and brokers need to replay the whole log

Since the metadata manager in tiered storage is pluggable, it's possible to implement a new one without changing interfaces that is better optimized for small remote log segments.

Topic Switching

Migrating classic topics to diskless have been mentioned in previous KIPs as it is an important feature. Switching classic topics to diskless would mean that there will be an offset chosen by the leader as the swtich-over point. From this point on logs are in diskless format and before that they are in classic format but they become consolidated diskless topics, so eventually these logs move to tiered storage while keeping their log format.

Summary

KIP-1150 introduced diskless topics. KIP-1163 defines their produce, fetch, and replica behavior, and KIP-1164 defines the Diskless coordinator. Those KIPs use mixed-partition write-ahead log (WAL) objects as the durable ingest format and leave the transfer to KIP-405 Tiered Storage to a follow-up KIP.

This KIP defines that transfer. Every diskless topic is a consolidated diskless topic (CDT) from creation. Producers write through the diskless WAL. Each assigned replica materializes the untiered suffix as ordinary per-partition Kafka log segments. The partition leader copies closed segments through the existing KIP-405 Remote Storage Manager (RSM) and Remote Log Metadata Manager (RLMM) interfaces. After the remote copy becomes durable and discoverable, the Diskless coordinator removes the matching WAL batch coordinates. KIP-405 then provides long-term storage, reads, and physical retention for the consolidated prefix.

This KIP also defines the offset frontiers, failure ordering, replica recovery, retention, and coordinator records needed to prune WAL data without losing or hiding records.

This KIP changes two earlier sketches:

  • KIP-1163 currently points its WAL-object merging section at KIP-1165. This KIP supersedes that reference. WAL-object merging is not part of KIP-1165.
  • KIP-1150 lists KIP-1163 and KIP-1164 as the minimum implementation. Because every upstream diskless topic consolidates from creation, KIP-1165 joins that minimum dependency set.

Motivation

The WAL is an ingest format

A WAL object combines batches from many topic partitions. This lets one object-storage upload cover many Produce requests and keeps the number of uploads independent of the partition count. The format is efficient for ingest, but it is a poor long-term per-partition log:

  • A lagging consumer needs coordinator lookups and ranged object reads to reconstruct one partition.
  • The Diskless coordinator retains one coordinate for every live WAL batch.
  • A reassigned replica must rebuild from mixed-partition objects.
  • Physical deletion of one partition's expired data waits for every other live batch in the shared object.

Kafka already has a long-term format

KIP-405 stores ordinary Kafka log segments. Existing RSM and RLMM plugins, remote reads, leader-epoch indexes, transaction indexes, producer snapshots, local retention, and operational tools already use that format.

Materializing WAL batches into Kafka segments lets diskless ingest reuse this storage system without teaching KIP-405 plugins about mixed-partition WAL objects.

The intuition for implementing this is to use something similar to the replica fetchers, except it fetches from the object storage, starting from the earliest WAL objects. This is called the Consolidation Fetcher. It extends the abstract classes in Kafka. It has the following main components:

How a record moves

Produce

A broker buffers batches, uploads one shared WAL object, commits the batch coordinates, and acknowledges the produce after the coordinator assigns offsets and advances D. That broker does not have to be the KRaft partition leader. The leader's job in this KIP is the KIP-405 copy, remote retention, and the coordinator updates that follow from them.

Materialization stays off this path. Writing the local log before the acknowledgement would put disk latency back on produce.

Materialize

Each assigned replica appends WAL batches to its local log in coordinator offset order, through the normal follower append path, so the batches keep the assigned offsets and timestamps. The local log is a cache and a staging area for tiering.

An idle partition still has to roll its active segment. KIP-405 only uploads a closed segment, so a non-empty active segment is rolled after segment.ms even when no later record arrives. Size-based rolling still uses segment.bytes. Rolling makes the last batches eligible for copy. It does not promise that the WAL object disappears within that time. Pauses and outages still delay the rest of the pipeline.

Copy

The leader uploads closed segments in offset order through the existing Remote Storage Manager and Remote Log Metadata Manager. A segment counts as remotely readable after the data, indexes, and producer snapshot are stored and the metadata manager has committed COPY_SEGMENT_FINISHED. The leader also checks that the new segment continues from S = max(G, T + 1) with no gap. An overlap on a batch boundary is allowed. Only then does T advance.

After a restart or a leadership change, the leader rebuilds T from the coordinator and from the finished remote segments. A larger remote end offset that skips a hole does not become T. If the leader's own local log starts after S, it rebuilds that missing live range before it uploads anything further.

Prune

The leader periodically tells the coordinator how far the gap-free remote prefix now reaches. The coordinator checks that the caller is the current partition leader, that the value is below D, and that the value does not move T backward. The coordinator cannot see plugin metadata itself, so this report is the leader's claim that it has checked the finished segments. After the coordinator record commits, it advances T, drops WAL coordinates at or below T or below G, and sets W to the first coordinate that remains.

A retry of an older value returns the stored state. Empty WAL objects are deleted with the KIP-1164 handoff. This KIP does not add a second object cleaner.

The order is the safety property. The remote copy, including the producer snapshot, is durable and visible before the WAL coordinate disappears. The other order can leave a hole: the last readable copy is the one that was just deleted.

Reads

A broker loads G, W, T, and D from the coordinator before it serves a CDT after startup or reassignment. If the coordinator is unavailable, the broker returns a retriable error and waits. A stale-low start would let a follower return records that DeleteRecords has already removed.

For a fetch offset that falls inside [G, D), the broker prefers the local log when that offset is actually in the local interval. Otherwise it reads KIP-405 when the offset is in [G, T], and the WAL when the offset is at or above W. An offset below G or above D is out of range. An offset equal to D is an empty success. If none of the three copies covers a live offset, the broker fails the partition closed and records a continuity violation.

A single Fetch response may start in the local log and continue into the WAL. The WAL portion starts at the next offset after the last local batch that was read. A size limit can stop the local read early. Continuing at the local log end in that case would skip the unread local batches.

ListOffsets(EARLIEST) is G. ListOffsets(EARLIEST_LOCAL) stays the serving replica's local log start. It is not W, because the WAL is object storage and EARLIEST_LOCAL means the local log. ListOffsets(LATEST) is D until transactional produce exists. Responses that carry a leader epoch use storage epoch 0. The KRaft epoch is used to fence the request.

OffsetsForLeaderEpoch fences on the KRaft epoch. A request for storage epoch 0 is answered with end offset D.

Retention

retention.ms and retention.bytes apply to one logical log: the remote prefix plus the WAL batches that are still the only copy(overlapping copies count once). The partition leader computes that decision, the Diskless coordinator records it and the Remote Log Manager deletes the remote objects afterward. The stock RLMExpirationTask does not choose the new start, because the local log begins at S and its size includes a cache the logical log must not count.

Leader

The leader builds the logical log from the remote segment catalog and the coordinator's remaining WAL batches. It applies retention.ms and retention.bytes oldest first and chooses a new global log start G. A compressed batch stays until its last offset falls below that start. Local segments are left out of the byte count.

The same pass runs while consolidation is paused. It can move G through WAL batches that were never copied. A replica whose local log now ends below the new G rebuilds from S.

Coordinator

The leader commits the new G with DisklessAdvanceLogStart. In that update the coordinator:

  • Makes every offset below G unreadable.
  • Drops WAL coordinates below G and recomputes W.
  • Returns the stored start when a retry asks for the same or a lower offset.

Replicas learn G on the metadata-only Fetch and reject reads below it. ListOffsets(EARLIEST) returns it.

If the commit fails, the old G stays and the leader deletes no remote objects. Expired bytes can remain readable through the outage. The next pass retries the same commit.

Remote Log Manager

After the commit, the leader asks the Remote Log Manager to delete each remote segment whose end offset is below G. A segment that still contains offsets at or above G stays. T does not move backward.

For each selected segment the Remote Log Manager marks DELETE_SEGMENT_STARTED, deletes the object through the remote storage manager, and marks DELETE_SEGMENT_FINISHED. A segment left in DELETE_SEGMENT_STARTED is deleted on a later pass because its end offset is still below the committed G.

Local segments

local.retention.ms and local.retention.bytes delete only broker-local cache segments. They do not delete remote objects or WAL objects, and they do not move G.

DeleteRecords

DeleteRecords uses the same split with a caller-supplied start. The offset -1 means D. The coordinator moves G forward to max(G, requestedOffset), drops WAL coordinates below that start, and recomputes W. A retry at the same or a lower offset leaves the committed start in place.

The request completes when every live replica that contributes to the low watermark has applied the new G. The Remote Log Manager then deletes remote segments below that G asynchronously, through the same segment delete it uses for retention.

Compatibility, deprecation, and migration plan

Existing clusters

The new feature and broker flag default to disabled. Classic and tiered-classic topics keep their current behavior. Clients do not need an upgrade.

KIP-1163 and KIP-1164 are still under discussion, so this KIP changes their initial diskless topic model before release. Upstream does not create a pure-diskless compatibility state.

Rolling upgrade

Operators use this sequence:

  1. Upgrade every controller and broker.
  2. Raise metadata.version to the latest.
  3. Configure and verify KIP-405 RSM and RLMM plugins.
  4. Enable diskless.system.enable=true and remote.log.storage.system.enable=true.
  5. Create CDTs with diskless.enable=true.

Downgrade

Software that does not support the metadata.version that ships this feature cannot replay the new coordinator records or serve a remote-only CDT prefix.

A cluster may lower metadata.version below the diskless version only before it creates its first CDT. Once the Diskless coordinator has written records from this KIP, downgrading is unsupported. An operator who needs older binaries must migrate the remaining topics to a new cluster. A future KIP may add an offline state-conversion procedure.

Deprecation

This KIP does not deprecate an existing released client API.

Rejected alternatives

Keep pure-diskless topics

A pure mode makes the WAL a second long-term storage system and leaves the coordinator proportional to retained data. It also creates topic transitions and mixed-version states that the initial upstream release does not need.

Operators can pause consolidation temporarily with the byte-rate limit. A pause is an operational state of a CDT, not a different topic type.

Merge WAL objects

Merging improves locality inside the WAL, but it does not produce per-partition Kafka segments, reduce the coordinator to an untiered suffix, or reuse KIP-405 reads and retention. This KIP therefore replaces the WAL-merging scope previously associated with KIP-1165.

Teach KIP-405 plugins to read WAL objects

This would require RSM and RLMM plugins, remote Fetch, and Kafka segment tools to understand mixed-partition WAL layout. Materializing Kafka segments keeps the plugin interfaces and remote format unchanged.

Materialize on the Produce path

Appending to UnifiedLog before acknowledging Produce restores local-disk pressure to the latency-sensitive path. Asynchronous consolidation preserves the KIP-1163 ingest model.

Further Improvements

Unified remote log metadata manager

With the current design only by plugging in RLM, a bottleneck is possible when remote logs roll over too fast. __remote_log_metadata has 50 partitions by default and every broker needs to fetch subscribe to all because partitions are scattered across all of them. This means that we need to improve the tiered storage remote log metadata management, to solve these problems:

  • limit inter-broker metadata traffic: on high frequency rollover, metadata is generated fast, which may generate inter-zone traffic, thus defeating some of the cost savings given by diskless topics.
  • better compaction: the current remote metadata log isn't compacted at all, so it can grow huge
  • improve snapshotting: tiered storage metadata has no compaction and brokers need to replay the whole log

Since the metadata manager in tiered storage is pluggable, it's possible to implement a new one without changing interfaces that is better optimized for small remote log segments.

Topic Switching

Migrating classic topics to diskless have been mentioned in previous KIPs as it is an important feature. Switching classic topics to diskless would mean that there will be an offset chosen by the leader as the swtich-over point. From this point on logs are in diskless format and before that they are in classic format but they become consolidated diskless topics, so eventually these logs move to tiered storage while keeping their log format.

Transactions

The current Diskless design doesn't include transactions and this is a further improvement path that Diskless needs to solve.
